title: Pennsylvania Town Pushes Back Against Developer's $10,000 Per Household Offer for Data Center
snippet: NorthPoint Development offered thousands in direct cash checks to Hazle Township residents to build a 1,300-acre data center, but locals are calling the deal an unwanted bribe.
content:
A real estate developer attempting to construct a massive data center in eastern Pennsylvania has escalated its charm offensive with an unprecedented proposal: writing $10,000 checks directly to every household in town.

NorthPoint Development hopes the financial incentive will convince residents of Hazle Township, located in the Pocono foothills, to approve a 1,300-acre facility. On top of the individual cash offers, the company dangling an additional $120 million over 15 years for local services, including improvements to public schools and emergency infrastructure.

Locals Call Direct Cash Offer a 'Bribe'

Despite Hazle Township’s median household income hovering around $60,000, the five-figure payout has met overwhelming resistance from the community. Many residents view the direct checks less as a generous offer and more as an insult or a bribe meant to silence legitimate community complaints.

Locals opposing the development cite a growing list of grievances, chief among them the continuous hum of noise pollution generated by cooling fans, rising electricity and water costs, declining home values, and a general skepticism toward both AI executives and local officials.

A Changing Tactic for Big Tech Expansion

Historically, developers seeking municipal approval for industrial projects offer funding packages to local governments to build infrastructure or improve public services. Distributing direct cash payouts to private citizens represents a novel and aggressive shift in tactics, likely born out of a chaotic public hearing last year where frustrated residents demanded to know how the project benefited them directly.

Despite the lucrative financial offers, NorthPoint faces a steep legislative battle. Hazle Township officials previously rejected the project on zoning grounds last year and subsequently enacted a temporary moratorium on all data center construction within the municipality. For now, the promise of cash is proving insufficient to overcome residents' quality-of-life concerns.
